content.text: A subclass that compiles isn't automatically substitutable. Barbara Liskov and Jeannette Wing define subtyping by behavior: a subtype must keep every promise callers can rely on from its supertype. It can accept more and guarantee more, but never demand more, deliver less or throw exceptions callers weren't told about. The compiler only checks signatures.

The belief: if a class inherits from a base class, or implements an interface, and the code compiles, then it can be used anywhere the base type is expected. The Liskov Substitution Principle is satisfied by construction.

It's a reasonable belief because the compiler does check a lot: method names, parameter and return types, overrides, accessibility. Liskov and Wing agree that's required: "Clearly subtypes must provide the expected methods with compatible signatures." Many tutorials also teach LSP as a rule about class hierarchies, and Robert C. Martin admits: "People (including me) have made the mistake that this is about inheritance."
The half-truth: compatible signatures are necessary. As the paper puts it, though, type checking "captures only a small part of what it means for a program to be correct".
Substitutability is about what callers can tell

Liskov and Wing's 1994 paper frames the question this way: objects of a subtype "ought to behave the same as those of the supertype as far as anyone or any program using supertype objects can tell." Their Subtype Requirement says that any property provable about objects of the supertype must also hold for objects of the subtype. Martin's 2020 phrasing of the
is shorter: "A program that uses an interface must not be confused by an implementation of that interface."
Signatures can't tell a stack from a queue
The paper's own example: a stack and a queue can both have a
that adds an element and a

that removes one. By the signature rules, either could be a legal subtype of the other. But "a program written in the expectation that x is a stack is unlikely to work correctly if x actually denotes a queue, and vice versa." Same shape, different behavior, and the compiler can't see the difference.
The paper turns "behaves the same" into checkable rules for each method the subtype provides:

content.text: It's not about inheritance at all

The paper notes that a subtype providing a supertype's methods doesn't mean it inherits their code, "simply that it provides methods with the same behavior". Martin makes the same point from the other side: LSP is about subtyping, all implementations of interfaces are subtypes of the interface, and duck types are subtypes of an implied interface. His warning about the cost: if an implementation confuses the user of the base type, "if/switch statements will proliferate."
The fix: promise only what every implementation keeps

blocks.title: Run the base type's tests against every implementation

content.text: Write the contract as tests against the base type in an abstract test class, then add one small subclass per implementation that supplies the instance. A new implementation that can't pass the shared tests isn't a subtype, whatever the compiler says.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Split promises that not everyone keeps

content.text: When an implementation can't honor part of a contract, give that part its own interface, or use composition instead of inheritance.

items.text: LSP is about behavior: code that uses a type must not be surprised by any of its subtypes.
Compatible signatures are necessary but not enough; a stack and a queue can share them.
A subtype may accept more and promise more, never demand more, deliver less or throw new exceptions.
It applies to interfaces and duck types, not only to class inheritance.
Type checks against subtypes and overrides that refuse to work are signs the contract is wrong; split it.
